sentences.text: The holotype — the specimen the species is based on — includes a partial upper jaw with ten teeth, six neck and back vertebrae, shoulder blades, arm bones, and most of the right hindlimb.
Its femur measures 166 cm in length, while the humerus is 149 cm long.
The relatively long front legs, with a humerus-to-femur ratio of 0.9, indicate that this trait is not exclusive to Brachiosaurids.
Researchers distinguished the species from other sauropods using unique features of its vertebrae, such as narrow neural spines and unique laminae on the neck bones.
Gregory S. Paul estimated the animal reached a length of 18 meters and a mass of 20 tons.
The genus name honors Giancarlo Ligabue, and the species name honors geologist Dr. Héctor A. Leanza, who discovered the skeleton.
The holotype specimen was found during a 1997 expedition at Cerro de los Leones, located 10 km west of Picún Leufú.
The species Ligabuesaurus leanzai was named in 2006 by José Bonaparte, Bernardo González Riga, and Sebastián Apesteguía.
A second skeleton, specimen MCF-PHV-228, was referred to the genus in 2022.
Researchers suggest that multiple fragmentary specimens found at the site likely belong to a single individual due to a lack of repeated bone elements.
Later analyses classified the genus as a non-titanosaur member of the group Somphospondyli.
The animal lived in the Early Cretaceous period in what is now Argentina.
It lived approximately 112 to 109 million years ago during the Aptian and Albian stages of the Early Cretaceous.
The fossil record dates the animal to between 113.2 and 110.1 million years ago.
The habitat shared with other sauropods like Limaysaurus, Comahuesaurus, and Agustinia.
Some analyses suggest it is a true titanosaur because it is a close relative of Andesaurus, while others classify it as a non-titanosaur somphospondylian.
